«Плуг и молот».finding: «Плуг и молот» ('Plough and Hammer') is a shabby consumer cooperative (потребкооператив) in the fictional provincial town of Stargorod in Ilf and Petrov's 'The Twelve Chairs' (1928); it is named twice — a rooster crows at noon in its yard in Ch. 1, and in Ch. 3 it reopens after a three-week inventory closure, and its counter clerks dump a barrel of rotten cabbage that later ruins Father Fyodor's rabbit-breeding scheme. The name is not a neutral shop sign: a crossed plough and hammer on a red star was the actual emblem of the Red Army from 1918 to 1922, before being replaced in 1922–23 by the now-canonical hammer and sickle. Set in the NEP years, the novel turns this into a small anachronistic joke — an already-superseded piece of grand revolutionary iconography stuck on a sleepy, inefficient backwater shop, part of the book's running gag of pompous institutional names on shabby institutions. Published translations already carry this across: the widely circulated English text renders it 'Hammer and Plough co-operative' (word order flipped to echo 'hammer and sickle'), and a published Chinese translation renders it 犁与锤, matching the zh rendering proposed for this edition.
«Плуг и молот».note_for_reader: The name echoes 'plough and hammer', the Red Army's own emblem before it was replaced by the hammer and sickle in 1922–23 — by the novel's NEP-era setting, an already old-fashioned piece of revolutionary iconography on a shabby small-town shop.
«Плуг и молот».rationale: Translated rather than transliterated in all three languages to keep the denotation (a consumer cooperative) and the connotative echo of the Red Army/hammer-and-sickle emblem; for English, flipped the word order to 'Hammer and Plough' to match the idiomatic 'hammer and sickle' pattern and sharpen that echo, giving up strict word-order fidelity to the Russian original.

«Сделал свое дело — и уходи».finding: The phrase is a stern printed poster hanging on the wall of the ZAGS (civil registry office) where Ippolit Matveyevich works as a registrar, part of the sensory catalogue of that office (the smell of alizarin ink, a wheezing clock, and this sign) that intimidates a young couple coming in to register their marriage. It belongs to a genre Ilf and Petrov mock throughout their work: the terse, categorical imperative signage of Soviet institutions ('No smoking', 'No entry without business', etc.) — the two writers even devoted a separate 1932 feuilleton, titled with this same catchphrase, to ridiculing that bureaucratic-command style of speech. The wording also echoes, without naming it, the much older Russian catchphrase 'Мавр сделал своё дело, мавр может уходить' ('The Moor has done his job, the Moor can go'), from Schiller's Fiesco, used in Russian to mean someone is discarded the moment they've served their purpose — so the bland productivity-poster surface carries a faint undertone of people being disposable once used, which is why it lands as a running joke rather than mere set-dressing. I could not find any established English/Chinese/Japanese rendering of this exact line tied to press coverage of Pavel Durov's 2013-2014 departure from VKontakte (searched directly); that connection, if intended by the task brief, is not attested in what I could retrieve, so I am flagging rather than inventing it.

rendering.en: "Once you've done your job, get out"
rendering.ja: 「用が済んだら、さっさと帰れ」

«Сделал свое дело — и уходи».note_for_reader: A wall poster in the office where the two heroes work, first of several — the same terse office-command style Ilf and Petrov mock elsewhere in their writing.
«Сделал свое дело — и уходи».rationale: Kept the denotation (finish the task, then leave) and the poster-terse, mock-solemn register identically in all three languages so the recurring gag reads the same at every occurrence; gave up any explicit trace of the underlying 'Мавр сделал своё дело' proverb (disposability once you've served your purpose), since spelling that out would turn a one-line sign into an explanation and the joke works on the surface reading alone.

«Нимфа».finding: «Нимфа» is the name-sign of the rival funeral/coffin shop in Chapter 1 of Ilf and Petrov's 1928 novel «Двенадцать стульев» — the chapter itself is titled «Безенчук и „нимфы“» ("Bezenchuk and the 'Nymphs'"). Its coffins are displayed 'silvering' behind wavy greenish glass on the left side of the street, in showy contrast to Bezenchuk's plain dusty oak coffins across the way; three interchangeable brothers co-own and run it, greeting Vorobyaninov in unison with mock-solemn courtesy about his mother-in-law's health. The joke is the mismatch between the shop's dainty, mythological, faintly Art-Nouveau signboard name — evoking beautiful Greco-Roman nature spirits — and its dowdy, provincial, morbidly businesslike owners and product (coffins). This mismatch, not any real connection to mythology, is what a 1920s Russian reader caught instantly from the sign alone. Established published translations render the name rather than transliterate its sound: John Richardson's English translation uses 'the Nymph Funeral Home' (confirmed against the lib.ru English text), and a 2022 Shanghai Translation Publishing Chinese edition (tr. 白桦熊) titles the chapter 第一章 别津丘克与「仙女」 — rendering «Нимфа» as 仙女 ('fairy/celestial maiden'), a domesticating choice that keeps the 'dainty supernatural beauty' connotation for a general Chinese readership rather than the more academic Greek-myth loanword 宁芙.
«Нимфа».note_for_reader: The shop's sign borrows a mythological name for beautiful nature-spirits — the joke is that its plain, businesslike coffin-sellers are anything but.
«Нимфа».rationale: For en and zh I bound to the rendering already established in a published translation (Richardson's 'Nymph'; the 2022 Shanghai Translation edition's 仙女) rather than inventing a new one — both translate the name's dainty/beautiful connotation over its bare sound, which is what the joke needs; zh trades the specifically Greek register of 宁芙 for the more broadly legible 仙女. No published Japanese rendering could be confirmed by search, so I kept the transliterated loanword ニンフ (a standard, well-understood Japanese term for Greek nymphs) as the best defensible choice, preserving denotation and connotation at the cost of the Cyrillic sound in all three languages.

Ипполит Матвеевич.finding: This is the first name and patronymic (no surname) of Ippolit Matveevich Vorobyaninov, the novel's protagonist: a former marshal of the nobility reduced under NEP to a clerk in a district registry office (ZAGS). In Russian, addressing or narrating someone by first-name-plus-patronymic alone is the standard polite/formal register used for adults of some standing; Ilf and Petrov use it relentlessly and almost exclusively for Vorobyaninov even as his circumstances become shabby, comic, and ultimately criminal, so the form itself becomes a running mock-solemn joke about a man clinging to a dignity the narrator (and the reader) knows is gone. English, Chinese and Japanese translations and secondary coverage of the novel consistently keep the name transliterated in full rather than substituting a bare first name or an anglicized title, confirming this is the settled convention rather than a contested choice.

rendering.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
rendering.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

Ипполит Матвеевич.note_for_reader: In Russian, calling an adult by first name plus patronymic (no surname) is the ordinary formal/polite address; the narrator's insistence on it for a man in increasingly undignified straits is part of the joke.
Ипполит Матвеевич.rationale: Kept denotation and the formal register by transliterating the full first-name-patronymic form in all three languages rather than collapsing it to a bare first name or a Western title, since none of the targets has a native equivalent of the patronymic convention; the ironic charge that a Russian reader feels automatically is given up unless flagged, which the translator's note partially restores.

conventions: Render Ипполит Матвеевич by full first-name-plus-patronymic throughout rather than switching to a bare first name or 'Mr. Vorobyaninov'; gloss the patronymic convention once, early, in a translator's note for zh/ja readers. [rank 1]

Keep товарищ and гражданин as distinct, consistent renderings ('Comrade'/'Citizen'; 同志/公民; 同志/市民) rather than collapsing both into a generic 'sir' or 'mister', since the choice between them marks social register and distance. [rank 1]
Render dialogue introduced by — as em-dash-led lines in en/zh; convert to standard JA quotation marks (「」) per Japanese convention, applied uniformly across the whole book. [rank 1]
Render dialogue turns with the Russian em-dash (—) opener in all three target languages rather than quotation marks, preserving the terse, play-like rhythm of the exchanges. [rank 0]

Keep the characters' foreign-language interjections (Бонжур, гут морген, маман, ондулянсион) transliterated/foreign-sounding in every target language rather than normalized to native equivalents, since the joke is the characters showing off borrowed words. [rank 0]

Default to "Ippolit Matveyevich" (name + patronymic, no surname) as the protagonist's running-narration form of address, reserving the full "Vorobyaninov" for introductions and formal contexts; since zh/ja have no patronymic system, use the same transliterated name+patronymic string consistently rather than switching to family-name-only address.
